For four years, a RAND project has counted the number of people living unsheltered in the Los Angeles neighborhoods of Hollywood, Venice, and Skid Row.

This new report contains updated findings and survey information: bit.ly/43n34MC

We're accepting applications for our new 1-year Master of Policy Analysis program at @RANDschooledu.

Apply now to join our first cohort this fall. ⬇️

Expert: Clearing the Strait of Hormuz of mines could be quick—if Iran isn't firing projectiles or sending out attack boats. But the effort could take months if that's not the case. bit.ly/4dnVpnn

New study: The overall number of unsheltered people in Hollywood, Skid Row, and Venice remained flat in 2025. But rough sleeping—sleeping without a tent, vehicle, or other shelter—rose by 20%, reaching its highest level in four years of monitoring. bit.ly/3PFgosH

International collaboration is a cornerstone of modern scientific research. But such collaborations can also be misused.

"We think that Iran has laid a relatively small number of mines. But it is extraordinarily difficult and slow to try to clear mines under fire."

We've been tracking trends in homelessness across Hollywood, Skid Row, and Venice.

New findings show that the overall number of unsheltered people in these LA neighborhoods remained flat in 2025, but rough sleeping reached its highest level in four years. bit.ly/49J4gO4

New episode of Policy Minded: bit.ly/49znRAr

New research: Homelessness holds steady across three L.A. neighborhoods as rough sleeping reaches a four-year high. bit.ly/4v1YVtp

New study on school cell phone policies ⬇️

Even in schools that ban phone use entirely, half of students said they still check their phones in class at least once a day. 

Roughly one-sixth said they do so more than five times per day. bit.ly/42Oz501
China is now on pace to end this century with 786 million fewer people than it has right now. That will have major consequences—for China and for its rivalry with the United States. bit.ly/42tu8JG

New RAND survey data show that about two-thirds of middle and high school English teachers assigned only one to four full books for students to read. bit.ly/4nt4Vce

This new report puts that evolution into perspective: bit.ly/4faxo4j
